summary: M. B. Cook, an American seaman from Friendship, Maine, made two voyages to Japan, the first at the time the Constitution was proclaimed in February 1889, and wrote these sketches for his family and friends. He describes arriving at Yokohama, riding in jinrikishas, restaurants, baths, and a theatre; excursions to Kamakura and the Dai Butsu and to Enoshima and its caves; Tokio, with its temples, Ueno Park, and the museum; the celebrations of the Constitution, to which a Japanese acquaintance invited him; a No dance, a cemetery, and cremation; and a later trip down the coast to Hiogo, Otsu, and Kioto. Between the scenes he retells legends and gives notes on education, newspapers, music, religion, dress, and the products of the country, much of it, as his introduction says, gathered from books and from what people told him.

notes_on_text: The author signs the introduction “M. B. C., Friendship, Maine, 1890”. He was very probably Melville Bradford Cook (1838–1927) of Friendship; no source found names him as the author in so many words.
